analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run health insurance plan to compete with private insurers on the ACA marketplaces.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have added a government-run insurance option to the health exchanges, was referred to a House subcommittee and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Affordable Care Act to require the Secretary of Health and Human Services to offer a government-run health insurance plan through the ACA exchanges starting in 2014, alongside private plans. The public plan would have to follow the same rules as private plans, charge premiums sufficient to cover its own costs, and would start with $2 billion in federal startup funding that it must repay over ten years. Its payment rates would initially match Medicare rates, with a 5% bonus for providers in the first three years, and it would use Medicare-style tools to keep costs down. Its backers said it would give consumers a cheaper choice and force private insurers to compete. It never got a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People buying health insurance through the ACA exchanges would gain a government-run plan that the bill directs to be low-cost, competing with private insurers and likely holding premiums down. Because the public plan would use Medicare-style payment rates, hospitals and insurers would face pressure to compete on price.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People buying insurance on the exchanges

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to offer a low-cost public health insurance plan through the ACA exchanges in every state, alongside private plans.

The plan must follow the same rules as private exchange plans (benefits, networks, cost sharing), offer bronze, silver, and gold tiers, and finance itself through premiums rather than ongoing appropriations, with $2 billion in startup funding repaid over ten years.
Authorizes the Secretary to use innovative payment methods — accountable care organizations, bundled payments, value-based purchasing — aimed at improving outcomes and controlling costs.
Applies Medicare's anti-fraud provisions (including the False Claims Act) to the public option and gives enrollees the same access to federal courts as Medicare beneficiaries.

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would face a government competitor, and hospitals and doctors would face Medicare-based payment rates (with a temporary 5% bonus in the first three years). Taxpayers front the $2 billion startup funding, which the plan must repay over ten years.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private insurers and health care providers

drawbacks.text: The public plan would have started with a $2 billion Treasury appropriation plus 90 days of claims reserves; while designed to be repaid over ten years, taxpayers bore the initial startup risk.

By basing early payment rates on Medicare rates, the plan would likely have paid hospitals and doctors less than private insurers do, which providers warned could reduce participation or shift costs elsewhere; the bill offered only a temporary 5% provider bonus to offset this.
Payment rates and methodologies were shielded from administrative and judicial review, limiting oversight of how the plan set what it paid for care.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — cheaper, more competitive coverage on the exchanges, and a check on private insurers — would have been broad, reaching everyone who buys coverage through the marketplaces. The main costs and risks are real but bounded by the bill's design: a $2 billion repayable startup appropriation, and the risk that a government plan set to Medicare-like rates could pay hospitals and doctors less than private insurers do, which providers argue could shift costs or limit choices. Critics also feared it could crowd out private plans entirely over time; supporters saw that as the point of competition. On balance it was a substantial, well-specified attempt to lower coverage costs, but it was never examined in committee or scored in a floor debate, so its actual effects were never tested in the legislative process.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee's Health Subcommittee three days after introduction and sat there with no hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 15, 2013 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On January 18, 2013, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where it remained with no further action.
No committee markup, floor vote, or Senate action ever occurred, and the bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, who avoided a government-run competitor on the ACA exchanges, and providers wary of Medicare-level payment rates.

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 50 cosponsors.

for.name: 50 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all Democrats, including senior members Henry Waxman and Frank Pallone.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after referring it to the Health Subcommittee.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Controlled committee chairs and floor scheduling, and the bill never advanced past subcommittee referral during the 113th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 50 cosponsors were Democrats, including some of the chamber's most senior Democrats, and no Republican supported it; the committee that buried it had a Republican majority.

industries.note: A government-run plan competing with private plans on the exchanges threatened to draw customers away and hold down premiums industry-wide. Insurers spent heavily against the public option during the 2009-2010 ACA debate and continued to oppose its revival.

Medicare-based payment rates would generally pay less than private insurance, but a 5% payment bonus for the first three years and automatic Medicare-provider participation were designed to win them over.

industries.industry: Health insurance customers on the ACA exchanges
industries.note: Not an industry, but the people buying coverage: they would have gained a cheaper competitor plan, which supporters argued would pressure private insurers to lower premiums.
